title: Semantic HTML: header, nav, main, section, article and footer

videos.script: Here are two versions of the bookshop's home page. {{both}} In a browser, you cannot tell them apart. Same logo, same menu, same two events, same address at the bottom. {{tree}} Now look at what a screen reader gets from each. The first is a flat run of text with three links in it. The second has a header, a menu, a main area, two articles with headings, and a footer. {{why}} The difference is one decision, made over and over. Every time a piece of content goes on the page, somebody chooses which element to put it in. A div says nothing. A nav says this is the site's menu. A heading says this is what the next part is about. {{jump}} Somebody who cannot see the screen uses exactly those words to move around. Jump to the main content. Next heading. List the links. On the first page, there is nothing to jump to. {{keys}} The lesson also covers the controls. A link takes you somewhere, and a button does something. A box that only looks like a button cannot be reached with the keyboard at all, and you will see that happen. {{axe}} At the end, a program called axe reads both pages and lists what is missing. It will not make the page right for you. It will tell you where to look. {{end}}
